entry.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

link.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

entry.content:
The general rule

Using technical jargon might make your abstract shorter - but it’ll take twice as long to read. Start the paper (abstract, intro) giving the readers some context on the problem you are trying to solve and on what is the state of solutions today, and USE VISUALIZATIONS.

Reading the abstract, a reader with no sufficient context on the innovations in the field (like myself) will be lost quickly (after being attacked by “content-dependent retrieval” and “single-stream softmax attention” in the first sentence, and the first architecture figure in page 7).

After doing some catching up, I think the main points of the paper could be described like so:

1. Residual streams could be upgraded to be non-uniform with attention

This is not a new contribution by the paper, but it is the main important context I was missing, and it’s one of the more interesting things I learned going over this paper. The credit for this idea (as far as I could tell) goes to Attention Residuals (AttnRes) (Kimi Team, 2026), which builds on earlier ways of letting a layer read all previous layers directly (Huang et al., 2017; Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025).

2. Attention over both depth AND tokens (/time)

A previous architecture - AttnRes - used attention on the residual stream of this same token. In this paper they expand this to both look across the different network layers as well as across each layer’s reaction to the previous tokens (here - up to 12 previous tokens). Another expansion of this idea is the use of multi-headed attention here. In this paper they use the convolution over the token history as the way to combine these. Here as well the idea isn’t novel (Mixture-of-Depths Attention attends over both tokens and earlier layers (Zhu et al., 2026), and short convolutions over previous tokens appear in Primer and Canon layers (So et al., 2021; Allen-Zhu, 2025)), but the use of convolutions for inter-token mixing in the depth attention is new as far as I could tell.

3. We made it work properly on production-sized models

Maybe the biggest contribution of the paper, in my view, is showing how they combined the first two points and using clever parametrization and caching they made it work on a large scale model, showing improvements over both vanilla architecture and previous attempts that scale to large models (not the biggest, but 18B and 28B are respectable models and not a model organism (even though this is the MoE total parameter count, not active)). Caveat that should be stated here - this is a properly sized model but the compute budget for training is much much smaller than that of a “proper” production size LLM.

How they could have done better

Maybe the paper isn’t aimed at outsiders, but as one trying to read it - bringing me “up to speed” wouldn’t have taken more than a few lines, written in simple english, and creating a more in depth view of their architectural suggestion (i.e figure 2, with a bit more focus on the architectural changes and most importantly - much earlier in the paper). Additionally, I thing the framing of attention over both depth (of the network) and over previous tokens jointly is more helpful (at least to me).

The main contribution of this paper are it’s results, which the paper presents in a very forward manner (abstract, first figure). They would be easier to understand given the context of the architectural changes.
entry.summary: They had a point, I'm sure it's buried in here somewhere.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract presents the technical details quite densely, making it difficult to immediately understand the motivation behind the method and what distinguishes it from previous approaches. I reorganized it to first introduce the problem, then explain the limitation of AttnRes and present MSAR as the proposed solution. I also improved the flow between the methodology, efficiency advantages, and experimental results.

Before and after

Before Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
After Deep Transformer models can struggle to effectively retrieve information from earlier layers, limiting the benefits of increasing network depth. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) address this challenge by using attention to retrieve information from previous layers, but rely on a single attention stream. We introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), which extends this approach by enabling multiple attention streams to independently retrieve information from previous layers. To create diverse streams without reducing the dimensionality of hidden representations, MSAR uses multi-scale causal convolutions that capture different ranges of sequence context. Each stream performs its own attention over previous layers, and the retrieved representations are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to produce a single input for the next layer. Furthermore, MSAR generates additional streams only when needed, avoiding the need to store or communicate multiple persistent representations. Experiments at the 18B and 28B MoE scales demonstrate that MSAR consistently outperforms standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes across all 12 downstream benchmarks. Scaling-law experiments further show a 1.58× compute speedup over standard residual connections at equivalent training loss, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results demonstrate that MSAR can improve the efficiency and performance of large-scale Transformer pre-training.

The general rule

Introduce the problem before describing the proposed method. Explain the limitations of existing approaches to establish why a new method is needed, then present the main contribution and how it addresses those limitations. Finally, highlight the most important experimental results. An abstract should communicate the motivation, novelty, and significance of a paper in a logical order without overwhelming readers with technical details.
entry.summary: A new approach to Transformer residual connections that improves performance while reducing the computational cost of deep learning.

entry.title: Critique of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals -“
entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper upgrades single-stream depth attention (AttnRes) into multi-head depth attention. It creates multiple streams from earlier layers by running short causal convolutions across neighboring tokens, lets each stream attend over depth independently, and mixes them back into a single layer input.

Strengths

MSAR generalizes single-stream depth attention into a multi-head retrieval mechanism, allowing layers to query earlier blocks through multiple parallel attention distributions and achieving strong scaling with minimal overhead.

Weaknesses

MSAR attributes its gains to multi-head depth attention, using 1D depthwise causal convolutions (K in {4, 8, 12}) to generate diverse source streams from neighboring tokens. However, injecting short causal convolutions into the residual path introduces explicit local sequence mixing before every Attention and MLP/MoE sublayer—an inductive bias already known to independently improve language modeling in architectures like Mamba and hybrid Transformers. In Table 2, removing the convolutions while keeping 4 query heads (w/o Conv) degrades Pile loss, nearly reverting to single-stream AttnRes. The authors interpret this drop as proof that depth-attention heads need source diversity, but it is equally consistent with the convolutions themselves doing the heavy lifting via local token mixing while the multiple depth queries add very little.

Verdict

Accept, as the empirical gains on 18B and 28B MoE models are strong, but the paper needs a control experiment adding the same convolutions to a single-stream baseline to verify that the gains actually come from multi-head depth routing rather than local token mixing.
entry.summary: One sentence summary of your take.

entry.title: Critique of of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Critique of of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper introduces MSAR, a new residual architecture that extends AttnRes by using multiple streams with different contextual views. The authors show improvements in training loss and downstream performance over Vanilla, mHC, and AttnRes, with relatively small computational overhead.

Strengths

Results are strong across both model scales and all 12 benchmark : MSAR improves over all three baselines on all 12 downstream benchmarks at both 18B and 28B model scales.

The paper considers practical efficiency, not just performance : adds only 0.3% activated parameters and 0.5% training FLOPs relative to Vanilla.

Weaknesses

It is not fully clear which component is responsible for the gains : The paper doesn’t show whether the gains come from multi-head depth attention or from the added convolutions and other architectural changes.

Figure placement: The main figure explaining the method appears only on page 7, rather than near the beginning of the paper.

How it could have been improved

Better isolate the contribution of multi-head depth attention from the convolutions.

Verdict

I would lean toward weak accept. The results are strong and the idea is interesting, especially given the small reported overhead. However, I would like to see more experiments explaining why MSAR works and whether the gains generalize beyond the tested models.
entry.summary: An interesting and efficient architecture with strong results, but its individual contributions could be better isolated.

entry.title: Follow-ups on Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
entry.content:
Follow-ups worth doing

Asymmetric Multi-Stream Residuals Across Sublayer Types

  • The Question: Can we significantly reduce the memory access bottleneck of MSAR by deploying multi-stream retrieval ($m=4$) exclusively before Attention sublayers, while keeping standard single-stream residuals before MLP sublayers?

  • The Experiment:
    1. Train a 10B MoE model using the architecture and Pile training budget described in Table 2 and Appendix A.
    2. Evaluate four configurations under identical training tokens and compute budgets:
      • Full MSAR (Default): $m=4$ streams applied to both Attention and MLP sublayers.
      • Asymmetric MSAR: $m=4$ streams prior to Attention sublayers; MLP sublayers bypass multi-stream expansion and the $\mathcal{H}^{Pre}$ mixer entirely, relying on standard single-stream residual connections.
      • Standard Baselines: Vanilla residuals and Block AttnRes as reference baselines.
    3. Measure the final pre-training loss on Pile, downstream benchmark scores, and wall-clock training throughput (tokens/sec) alongside memory I/O cost.
    4. Visualize the learned Pre-Attn depth-attention weights (replicating Figure 4) to verify that restricting MLP sublayers to a single stream does not degrade the cross-depth diversity of Attention sublayers.
  • Why it’s worth someone’s time: The authors identify memory access cost as the primary operational overhead of MSAR: Table 6 shows that forward-pass memory I/O reaches $21.5d$ per token per sublayer for Block MSAR, compared to only $5.5d$ for AttnRes and $3d$ for Vanilla. However, the attention weight visualizations in Section D (Figure 4) reveal a striking contrast: Pre-Attention reads retrieve broadly across historical blocks and utilize diverse streams, whereas Pre-MLP reads focus almost entirely on the local diagonal (the immediate preceding sublayer). Allocating $m=4$ full retrieval streams to MLP sublayers incurs heavy memory traffic for operations that show little cross-depth diversity. An asymmetric design directly eliminates this inefficiency, potentially preserving MSAR’s performance gains while drastically cutting memory bandwidth overhead.
entry.summary: Cutting memory bandwidth overhead via asymmetric residual stream allocation between Attention and MLP sublayers.

entry.title: The Illustrated Speculative Decoder
entry.content:
A single forward pass

A forward pass is multiplying every layer’s weight matrices against the input.

For one input you load all the weight matrices into SRAM (× 24). So it is cheaper to feed in a matrix holding all the tokens (= vectors) than one vector at a time.

The catch: at inference the model doesn’t know the next token until it computes it — so one vector goes in at a time. In contrast, at training the whole text is known in advance — so all the tokens go in at once. Speculative decoding is the way to exploit this at inference too (coming up…)

A model’s input and output

Input: a token, or several tokens at once. Output: a probability table for the next word, for every token that went in.

Speculative decoding

A small model guesses a few tokens ahead, one after another. The large model takes all of them at once and checks.

The gain: the large model gets several tokens in one forward pass — it loads its weights once, not once per token.

A draft that is part of the verifier

The paper: Matryoshka LM Suites.

The problem: in speculative decoding with two separate models, the draft has to be tiny — so that time is really saved. But a tiny draft guesses badly: it agrees with the large model less often, and more guesses are rejected.

What the paper proposes: train the draft and the verifier as one model — the draft is the first layers of the verifier, with its own head, and during training the large model distills into the small one.

What this gives:

  • The small model agrees with the large one more — same layers + distillation.
  • One model in memory, not two.
  • Per the paper: the verifier does not recompute the first layers — the draft already did.
  • So the draft can be larger than usual.

entry.title: A token pov through MSAR
entry.content:
The original

The original figure shows an abstract view of individual components, each activating on the sequence matrix, compared against AttnRes. For an unsuspecting reader, it might seem that the architectures are similar, and that MSAR is simply AttnRes but “more times”. This however is not the case, as the casual convolutions work along the sequence dimension rather then depth.

The redesign

What changed and why

The redesign is essentially a zoom-in of the original. Maintaining every component whilst emphasising the sequence-dimension activations.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract explains the method clearly, but it follows a conventional structure: background, motivation, architecture, implementation details, and finally results. The most compelling finding, that MSAR achieves a 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over standard residual connections, appears only in the final sentences.

This result is particularly interesting because MSAR improves the residual architecture without substantially increasing its computational cost. Yet the original abstract spends more space explaining architectural details than communicating the practical significance of the improvement.

My rewrite makes four changes:

  1. Lead with the quantitative result. Open with the 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup to immediately establish why the paper matters.
  2. Explain the problem before introducing terminology. Describe how standard residual connections accumulate information from previous layers, making earlier representations harder to retrieve selectively.
  3. Present the method as a simple progression. Explain how MSAR creates different contextual views, independently retrieves information across depth, and combines the results, without overwhelming the reader with implementation details.
  4. Quantify both performance and overhead. Include the improvement over AttnRes, the consistent gains across 12 benchmarks, and the negligible additional training FLOPs.

Before and after

Before Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
After Can changing how Transformer layers reuse earlier representations make language model pre-training substantially more compute-efficient? We show that Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) achieves a **1.58× iso-loss compute speedup** over standard residual connections, outperforming previous alternatives such as AttnRes (1.35×) and mHC (1.30×). Standard residual connections accumulate layer outputs into a single representation, making it difficult for deeper layers to selectively retrieve earlier information. While AttnRes addresses this through attention over network depth, it relies on a single retrieval stream. MSAR extends this idea to multi-head depth attention: lightweight causal convolutions create multiple full-dimensional views of earlier representations, each independently attends to historical layers, and adaptive mixing combines the retrieved information. To avoid the cost of maintaining multiple streams, MSAR stores only single-stream summaries and expands them when needed. Evaluated on 18B and 28B MoE models, MSAR outperforms standard residuals, mHC, and AttnRes across all 12 downstream benchmarks, while adding only **0.5% training FLOPs** at the 28B scale. These results suggest that more selective access to earlier representations can improve both model quality and pre-training compute efficiency without substantially increasing architectural overhead.

The general rule

Lead with the most compelling finding, not the method used to achieve it. An abstract should immediately communicate why the research matters before explaining how it works. A concrete, quantitative result gives readers a reason to care about the proposed approach.

In particular, when a paper introduces a new architecture, the abstract should first establish its practical significance, then briefly explain the problem it addresses and the key idea behind the solution. Supporting numbers should make the improvement tangible, while technical implementation details can be left for the main text.
entry.summary: MSAR's most compelling result, reaching the same training loss with substantially less compute, is buried at the end of the abstract. Here is a version that puts it first.

entry.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals, The Author’s Path.

link.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals, The Author’s Path.

entry.content:
A bit about the Authors’s path.

Xiaohan Qin (First Author)

Xiaohan Qin is a Ph.D. student in Computer Science at Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU). She completed her undergrad (CS) at SJTU in 2025 and now works at SJTU’s ReThinkLab and the School of Intelligent Instruments (SII). Her research focus is on neural network architecture and training improvements. Specifically, Transformer modeling and multi-task learning. Qin previously worked on papers like “Expanded Hyper-Connections” (xHC), which augments the Transformer’s residual streams for better capacity, as well as methods like JTok (token self-modulation) and NITP (Next Implicit Token Prediction) for more efficient language-model pretraining. She has also worked on multi-task fairness.

The current paper Multi-Stream Attention Residuals fits naturally into Qin’s trajectory: it is another architecture enhancement for Transformers that aims to improve training efficiency. In fact, she is listed as a co-author on related works like xHC (expanded hyper-connections). In summary, this paper continues her research within large language models and improvements to the Transformer’s architecture.

Junchi Yan (Last Author)

Junchi Yan is a professor (Distinguished Research Fellow) at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s School of Artificial Intelligence (and School of Computer Science). He earned his Ph.D. in electronic engineering from SJTU (2015, under Wei Liu) and has been on the SJTU faculty since. Yan is the founder and leader of SJTU-ReThinkLab (in partnership with the Shanghai Innovation Institute, SII). Under his leadership, ReThinkLab focuses on “cutting-edge technologies” combining data-driven learning with optimization: spanning areas like foundation LLMs, multi-task learning, and even quantum machine learning. For example, his recent publications include work on Hyper-Connections (coauthored with Qin and others), as well as on quantum neural operators and reinforcement learning topics.

This paper aligns with Yan’s general goal of improving deep learning architectures and their training. As co-author and lab director, Yan has steered many projects on Transformer scaling (e.g. Hyper-Connections, MoE upcycling, token scaling axes) and multi-objective optimization. Multi-Stream Attention Residuals continues in that diretion by proposing a new residual scheme for Transformers. Specifically, the idea of having multiple attention streams over previous layers extends the line of research (from manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections to attention-based residuals) that Yan has been involved in. In short, this paper represents the next step in the authors series of works on stronger residual connections and more efficient training for large models than that we currently have today, fitting squarely into Yan’s lab mission in machine learning and applications.
entry.summary: What you need to know about the authors's background.

entry.title: Making the MSAR methods section easier to follow

link.title: Making the MSAR methods section easier to follow

entry.content:
What I changed and why

I propose adding a table of operations and dimensions to the methods section to help readers trace the computation

MSAR involves contextual expansions that combine token positions, depth attention that combines earlier sources, and stream fusion that combines the retrieved views. Following these operations requires keeping track of what each index refers to and what shape each intermediate representation has.

Figure 2 shows the overall scheme, but it does not provide all the information needed to follow each transformation. A table showing the operations alongside their input and output dimensions makes the computation easier to follow.

I also write operations directly, avoiding additional symbols such as $E_{i,r}$, $\phi$, $q_l^{(r)}$, and $k_i^{(r)}$, because I think this makes it easier to keep track of each term.

Before and after

Before

The expanded streams serve as distinct depth-attention heads, each associated with a different contextual scale. For each target layer, we perform depth attention independently within each stream, aggregating the corresponding source representations across depth:

The retrieval is then defined in Eqs. (11)–(12). The next subsection begins:

The retrieved streams $Z_l$ must be fused into a single input for the target layer.

Equations (13)–(14) define that fusion. The proposed addition brings these steps, together with source expansion, into one view.

After

Add the following table:

MSAR architecture

Token index $t$ is omitted except where neighboring positions are explicitly used.

Stage Operation Input shape(s) Output shape
Collect sources $v_0=h_1$
$v_i=f_i(h_i)$, $1\le i<l$		 $S$ vectors of size $d$ $S\times d$
Expand sources $v_{i,t}^{(0)}=v_{i,t}$
$v_{i,t}^{(r)}=\sum_{\delta=0}^{\kappa_r-1}c_{i,r,\delta}\odot v_{i,t-\delta}$
$r=1,2,3$; $\kappa_r=4,8,12$		 Sources: $S\times d$
Each filter: $d$		 $S\times m\times d$
Score sources $s_i^{(r)}=(w_l^{(r)})^\top\mathrm{RMSNorm}(v_i^{(r)})$ Keys: $S\times m\times d$
Queries: $m\times d$		 $S\times m$
Normalize over sources $\alpha_{i\to l}^{(r)}=\dfrac{\exp(s_i^{(r)})}{\sum_{j=0}^{l-1}\exp(s_j^{(r)})}$ $S\times m$ $S\times m$
Retrieve across depth $z_l^{(r)}=\sum_{i=0}^{l-1}\alpha_{i\to l}^{(r)}v_i^{(r)}$
Stack the $m$ vectors as rows of $Z_l$		 Values: $S\times m\times d$
Weights: $S\times m$		 $m\times d$
Flatten and normalize $u_l=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{Flatten}(Z_l))$ $m\times d$ $1\times(md)$
Compute gates Projection + scale + bias → sigmoid
Produces $H_l^{\mathrm{pre}}$		 $1\times(md)$ $1\times m$
Form input $h_l=(H_l^{\mathrm{pre}}Z_l)^\top$ $Z_l$: $m\times d$
$H_l^{\mathrm{pre}}$: $1\times m$		 $d$
Compute output $v_l=f_l(h_l)$ $d$ per token $d$ per token

Block MSAR

Use block summaries rather than individual layer outputs. To do so, partition consecutive layers into blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_N$. For layer $l\in B_n$, use: | Source | Definition | Shape per token | |—|—|—| | Embedding | $b_0=h_1$ | $d$ | | Completed blocks | $b_j=\sum_{i\in B_j}v_i$
$j=1,\ldots,n-1$ | $d$ each | | Current partial | $b_n^{<l}=\sum_{i\in B_n,\ i<l}v_i$ | $d$ |

Apply the same operations to these sources.

The general rules

  1. Explain operations alongside their dimensions. In this way, the reader can follow how one stage’s output becomes the next stage’s input.
  2. Make the axis of the operation explicit, since we have token positions, depth, and streams
entry.summary: A table of operations and dimensions helps readers follow the architecture without losing track.
